beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. Researching a market usually eats a full day — reading and note-taking don't parallelize in one head. Point Claude at the same pile of sources and it compresses to about an hour. So what does that hour actually get you?

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. You might not call yourself a researcher, but if you've ever spent an afternoon reading up on a market you were about to enter, or pulled a competitor dossier before a pitch — that's the work. You've done it. It just never made it onto the calendar, because unpaid research always loses to visible work.

Here's what the default looks like. An afternoon vanishing into open tabs and printouts, trying to hold ten sources in one head — which no head is built for. Useful work, but slow, and easy to keep postponing. That's the design flaw people work around by not doing it.

Point research support at the same pile and the shape changes. Give it a topic and a set of sources and, in about an hour, you get what used to take a day. Here's what's actually happening: the bottleneck was never your intelligence — it was working memory and time. Machinery that reads in parallel doesn't fix the thinking; it clears enough room for you to do it.

production_viz.label: A DAY INTO AN HOUR
production_viz.caption: the bottleneck was time, not intelligence

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. Give Claude a topic and a stack of sources — articles, reports, documents — and it pulls out the common themes, the places they conflict, and the takeaways that matter. Sources in; structured understanding out. They optimized for reading across the pile, not for shrinking each item on its own.

Here's the difference that matters. It isn't reporting what each source says, one by one — it's telling you what they mean together. A stack of separate accounts becomes one picture: the throughline no single article stated on its own. That's a different job than summarizing, and the design assumes you want the second one.

production_viz.label: WHAT THEY MEAN TOGETHER
production_viz.caption: the throughline no single source stated

beats.narration_text: That's the line between summary and synthesis. A summary shrinks each source and hands you back a smaller pile — you still have to read across it yourself. Synthesis reads across for you. Only one of those is the version you can actually decide on.

production_viz.label: SUMMARY VERSUS SYNTHESIS
production_viz.caption: the version you can decide on

beats.narration_text: Pointed at your market, the same engine does four jobs. Competitor intelligence. A structured market review. Gap analysis — what's covered and what isn't. And citation tracking, so every claim keeps its source. One synthesis engine, four framings: they chose reusability over specialization.

Competitor intelligence first. Claude reads how rivals position themselves, what they're building, how they talk to customers — and where the gaps sit. It works from public information alone, and gets sharper the moment you drop their materials into your own folders. The trade-off: it can only see what's already been written down.

production_viz.label: READING THE RIVALS
production_viz.caption: public information, sharper with your files

beats.narration_text: What comes back is a map, not a list — and that's a deliberate design choice. Where each competitor sits on price and focus, who's crowded together in the same corner, and the corner nobody's standing in. That empty quadrant is often the whole point of the exercise. Hold onto it.

production_viz.label: THE EMPTY QUADRANT
production_viz.caption: often the whole point of the exercise

beats.narration_text: Every finding stays attached to where it came from. Ask for proper attribution and Claude tracks the sources and formats the citations, and it'll hook into a reference manager if you already run one. Here's what that costs: verbatim attribution only travels forward if you told the model to carry it. Ask, or the trail dies.

Gap analysis runs the same move on your own coverage. After reading across a topic, Claude shows what's been handled well and what's thin — in the market, or in your own research. You see the hole before it costs you. But 'thin' here means 'thinly represented in what I read.' Absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

production_viz.label: FIND THE HOLE
production_viz.caption: see it before it costs you

beats.narration_text: Most of this rides on how you ask. For a competitor deep dive, you'd type something like this: everything public on their positioning, pricing, audience, recent launches, customer sentiment — then the strengths and weaknesses. Specific in, specific out. Vague in, generic out. The machinery mirrors the prompt.

Or point it at a batch you've already collected. Drop a folder of articles into Cowork and ask for the trends they agree on, the places they disagree, and what it means for your situation specifically. Synthesis on your own shelf — where the sources are ones you've already vetted, which changes what you can trust the output for.

Say you're weighing a new market. Ask Claude to research it — how big, who's already there, what customers actually need, where the openings are — and back comes a structured briefing: context, players, pain points, opportunity gaps, watch-outs. Five sections in a fixed order — that's a template, not a thought. Yours is the thinking on top of it.

But the output is only as sharp as the purpose you name. 'Research AI trends' gets you a bland overview — the model has no way to weight what matters. 'Research AI trends so I can decide whether to add AI services to my practice' gives you focused, usable intelligence, because now it can prioritize. The purpose shapes the answer.

production_viz.label: PURPOSE SHAPES THE OUTPUT
production_viz.caption: name the decision, sharpen the answer

beats.narration_text: This is the moment research is really for — standing at the edge of a decision you can't take back, maybe eyeing that empty quadrant from the competitor map. This works if you value scouting before you commit; it fails if you needed a verdict handed to you. Either way: better to have walked the ground than to find out after you've stepped.

For a straight choice — free-trial versus freemium, say — ask for the advantages and drawbacks of each for your kind of product, with real examples. Claude lays them side by side on the evidence. That's the trade you're making: gut feeling for structured comparison, faster but only as good as the examples it found.

production_viz.label: OPTIONS, SIDE BY SIDE
production_viz.caption: a comparison, not a gut feeling

beats.narration_text: Here's the discipline, and it's the whole game. Treat what comes back as leads, not verdicts. A finding that matches what you expected doesn't confirm it's true — the scout can be confidently wrong. And a finding that surprises you doesn't confirm it's false either — it might be exactly the gap you needed to see. Either way: verify the load-bearing claims, check the sources, keep the judgment yours. That's the honest limit of the machinery — a fast reader, not a trustworthy witness.

production_viz.label: LEADS, NOT VERDICTS
production_viz.caption: matching isn't proof, surprising isn't disproof

beats.narration_text: And when sources disagree, don't smooth it over. Ask Claude to flag the contradictions and leave them standing. Experts disagreeing isn't a mess to clean up — it's a map of where the real uncertainty lives, and that's information you want. Averaging opinions is a design trap: it hides exactly the signal you came for.

production_viz.label: KEEP THE DISAGREEMENTS
production_viz.caption: a map of the real uncertainty

beats.narration_text: Which leaves one habit worth building. Picture the operator with their head down in delivery — shipping the work, never once looking up at the market moving around them. That's how you get outmaneuvered by someone who spent an hour reading.

Now picture the operator who spends an hour a month scouting — who knows their market cold. Same desk, window open. Roughly the same effort, sharper decisions. That's the whole return on the habit. Set the time aside, and let Claude do the reading.

So here's the carry-out. The research plugin turns your sources into synthesis, not summary — that's the actual move they built. But every finding it hands back is a lead to verify, never a verdict to trust outright. That last part isn't a caveat bolted on; it's the design being honest about what a fast reader can and can't be.

props.quote: Research support turns your sources into synthesis, not summary — but every finding it hands back is a lead to verify, never a verdict to trust outright.
props.sparkLine: Leads to verify, not verdicts to trust.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste right now into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no research plugin required — that runs a full scouting pass on the market you're eyeing. It sizes it, maps the players on the axes you care about, marks the empty quadrants, lists the real customer complaints with sources, and flags every claim it's not confident in. Go deeper: which of those empty quadrants is empty because nobody's tried it, and which is empty because someone tried and failed? How would you tell the difference?

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm about to enter [market or product area]. Act as my scout, not as a spokesperson for anyone in it. (1) Size the market: rough total, growth direction, and how you're estimating — if you're guessing, say so. (2) Map the main players on two axes I should care about (price and focus, or the axes you'd recommend), and mark the empty quadrants. (3) List the top three things customers in this space actually complain about, with the source I could go read to verify each. (4) Flag every claim you're less than 80% confident in, so I know what to verify before I commit. Keep synthesis, not summary — tell me what the sources mean together, not one by one.
